newsitem.title: UK: Branson still sees BA/American stranding.
newsitem.headline: Branson still sees BA/American stranding.

text.p: Richard Branson, entrepreneur and chairman of Britain's privately-owned Virgin Atlantic Airways, said on Wednesday he still expects the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines to founder.
"I honestly believe there is rude awakening ahead," he told Reuters, after the UK Office of Fair Trading said it had finally sent a competition study into the deal to the Trade Department.

Branson said that he did not expect Minister of Trade Ian Lang to allow the alliance, especially not in its present form. "I don't think they will clear BA/AA. They will either refer it, or put enormous restrictions on it," he said.
Branson said that, despite suggestions from the airline industry and the press to the contrary, he did not believe the deal was likely to be politically acceptable in Britain.
"I think there has been a lot of inaccurate press reports planted in the last week to try and give the impression that there is a momentum for this deal to go through."
He said approval with anything other than strict conditions "would be enormously counter to everything that John Bridgeman and Ian Lang have said about the need for strong competition."
Bridgeman is the director of fair trading at the OFT.
Branson also saw poor prospects for an "open skies" pact.
Pondering the possibility of the alliance being given the go-ahead by Britain, he said "if I am mistaken, then what it means is that BA has got over just one of many hurdles."
In particular, he doubted that the key bilateral air service agremeent, known as an "open skies" deal, would be achieved between Washington and London without some U.S. concessions.
He claimed to have received a personal assurance from Prime Minister John Major that Britain would stick to its guns in these talks, which have been suspended since August.
"The PM has written to me personally, saying they will never ...settle on terms that would be unacceptable to the British."

"There is a (UK) Department of Transport position," Branson added, "and I have been assured that the kind of open skies that Gemany agreed to (earlier this year), would be completely unacceptable to the British."

Virgin and other British airlines have noted that, in contrast to the content of the deal between the United States and Germany, they want British negotiators to insist on cabotage rights (giving access to the U.S. domestic market), ownership rights and the creation of a mechanism for policing competition.

Branson said that Lang's review, these "open skies" difficulties, the necessity of seeking immunity from U.S. anti-trust rules and the threat of a court action by BA's former U.S. partner US Air together presented a web of obstacles.
"My personal belief is that they will not get over all these hurdles," he said.
